title: Methods
text:
The experiment is located in the Jackson Demonstration State Forest in coastal northern California. Four harvest treatments were replicated at four sites in 2012: group selection (GS), high-density dispersed retention (HD), high-density aggregated retention (HA), and low-density dispersed retention (LD). The retained-overstory treatments targeted post-harvest relative densities of 13% or 21%; group selection created a 1-ha opening with a lightly thinned buffer. These treatments were designed to examine alternative pathways for developing multiaged redwood stands (Berrill & O’Hara, 2009; Reineke, 1933).
Ten years after harvest, regeneration plots and fuel transects were established within each 0.2-ha treatment macro plot. Regeneration measurements characterized redwood, tanoak, and Douglas-fir; fuel transects characterized dead surface fuels and live vegetation. The plots were remeasured after precommercial thinning, which released selected conifers from competing trees and shrubs.



Detailed sampling procedures, model diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses will be retained as supplementary material.


Basal area was modeled separately for redwood, tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species using zero-inflated Gamma mixed models with a conditional log link. Treatment was a fixed effect; site and macro plot nested within site were random intercepts. Each species category had its own intercept-only zero and dispersion components. Each model used 64 vegetation-plot observations from four sites and 16 macro plots. Arithmetic mean basal area included modeled zeros and integrated over both fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. Confidence intervals for the means were calculated using the log-scale delta method with the full parameter covariance, including random-effect variance uncertainty. Redwood and tanoak estimates are displayed in the Results; estimates for all four categories are reported in the supplement.



Reported values are model-based arithmetic mean loads, including modeled zeros and integrating over fitted random effects, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts.
These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

title: Discussion
text:
Discussion
The discussion will first interpret regeneration responses in relation to the silvicultural objective of developing a new redwood cohort beneath varying levels of retained overstory. It will then interpret phase-specific fuel conditions and the PCT-associated contrast as a linked management question, with conclusions limited to the reviewed sampling design and analysis.
This structure treats silviculture and fire management as linked management questions while keeping conclusions within the support of the reviewed analyses and cited literature.

title: Abstract
text:
Abstract
Forest managers using retention forestry need information on regeneration and fuel development to design productive stands in fire-adapted ecosystems. We analyzed 10-year remeasurement data from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment in Jackson Demonstration State Forest, California. The experiment compared group selection, aggregated retention, and low- and high-density dispersed retention treatments and measured regeneration, sprout growth, and surface fuel loading.
Redwood regeneration responded strongly to increasing canopy openness, whereas tanoak responses were more modest. Sprout-height findings will remain part of the main regeneration evidence. Fuel measurements describe conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including the PCT-associated contrast. The manuscript will evaluate how overstory retention affects regeneration while presenting fuel components in a form useful for integrated silviculture, fuels, and fire management.

title: RT03 — fuel Results narrative
text:
Implemented source and review decisions







Source or finding
Implementation in RT03




Thesis analysis/thesis/results.qmd, fuel subsections
Retain the pre-PCT, post-PCT, and vegetation-transition sequence, using current publication values throughout.


Revised component definitions
Report woody and herbaceous vegetation separately; distinguish modeled litter and duff before PCT; omit post-PCT forest-floor estimates.


RD04 inference review
Use equally site-weighted, random-effect-integrated arithmetic mean loads including zeros, rather than the thesis zero-random-effect references.


Joint woody phase model
Report its four pre-minus-post mean reductions and covariance-aware confidence intervals, consistent with the woody load panel. Do not use the separate Student-t difference-model estimates.


Thesis significance and causal wording
Replace inherited p-values with descriptive treatment rankings. Report exclusion of zero only for the four computed woody-change intervals; dead-fuel phase comparisons have no paired-change tests here.


Slash and design interpretation
Describe potential surface-fuel contribution, not measured slash deposition; avoid attributing the entire phase transition to PCT.


Numerical provenance
Draw inline narrative values and the shared companion table from rd04-fuel-model-estimates.csv; do not carry forward the unsourced coarse-wood grand mean noted in the audit.



Review products: the fuel Results draft, existing nine-panel figure and caption, and the companion values table. The table source is sections/rd04-fuel-estimates-table.qmd; it can be moved to an appendix without changing the numerical source.
Acceptance tests: each quantitative claim is traceable to the current figure/CSV; point-estimate rankings are not presented as pairwise tests; intervals describe uncertainty in means, not new-transect variation; the standing-woody contrast is not a direct slash measure or an isolated causal PCT effect. Scientific model acceptance and table placement remain open for review. RT03 is not marked accepted or complete by drafting it.

title: Task register and task list
text:
Task list

F01 — fuel-component separation and model exploration
Status: Completed — analytical record.
The component definitions separate vegetation components and pre-PCT litter/duff, omitting post-PCT forest-floor estimates. The analytical source review contains derivation, exploration, candidate-fitting code, and their complete CSV outputs. The model-review register reports provisional AIC leaders, not final selections. Prediction, inference, and display decisions belong to RD04; the pipeline map links the complete sequence.


RD04 — fuel phase and PCT display
Status: Figure complete; companion table pending review.
The nine-panel inventory reports phase-specific fuel loads and a matched woody-vegetation contrast. The inference review compares thesis and publication predictions and documents the switch to random-effect-integrated means, with woody change derived from the joint phase model and its pre/post covariance. A companion table reformats all 60 estimates from the canonical CSV. Model assumptions and final table placement remain under review. The complete source and output review owns the inference-audit and figure scripts, retired implementation, and all audit/estimate CSVs; F01 supplies the fitted-model record.


RD02 — regeneration basal-area/density display
Status: Separate models selected; displays pending review.
The overall sensitivity review examines joint random-effect structures and same-data species comparisons; the focused RW/TO comparison examines separate fitting and species-specific variances. The recorded selection uses four separate zero-inflated Gamma models with site and nested macro-plot intercepts. Prediction, gradient, integration, and optimizer checks accompany the RW/TO Results figure and all-category supplement estimates; display review remains open.


RD03 — sprout-height display
Status: Queued.
The proposal reviews treatment, temporal, and 10-year redwood/tanoak sprout-height displays together, retaining the smallest set that preserves their distinct messages. The task page identifies the three thesis source figures and requires the chosen display to distinguish treatment from time without repeating the basal-area/density result.


RT01 — regeneration Results narrative
Status: Queued — after RD02.
After RD02 acceptance, the proposal is to draft a 1–2-page regeneration Results subsection around the accepted display, emphasizing redwood with concise tanoak context and supplemental treatment of other species. Every quantitative claim must be traceable to an accepted display or linked table.


RT02 — sprout-height Results narrative
Status: Queued — after RD03.
After RD03 acceptance, the proposal is to report redwood and tanoak height/time findings in a distinct 1–1.5-page Results subsection. Combining it with RT01 remains conditional on one shared display and a clearer common message; the narrative must add sprout-development evidence without restating basal-area/density findings.


RT03 — fuel Results narrative
Status: Pending review.
The fuel Results draft follows the thesis pre-PCT, post-PCT, and vegetation-transition sequence using current publication values. The source and review decisions document separated components, integrated means, covariance-aware woody changes, and replacement of inherited significance claims with descriptive rankings. Inline values and the companion table share the canonical CSV; the draft remains pending review, with explicit limits on slash and causal PCT interpretations.


MD01 — study design display
Status: Queued — Methods stage.
The proposed design display combines study area, treatment layout, and sampling logic if the result remains legible, with the second map or layout moved to the supplement. Its review criterion is that readers can identify the four treatments, replication, and measurement phases without consulting the text.


M01 — study area and experimental design
Status: Queued — after MD01.
Following MD01 acceptance, the proposal retains the setting, four treatments, replication, timing, and PCT context needed to understand the accepted results. A 1–1.5-page Methods subsection and compact design table should make every displayed variable and phase traceable to the experimental design.


M02 — regeneration and sprout methods
Status: Queued — after RT01/RT02.
The proposal describes the regeneration and sprout measurements and analyses retained in accepted displays, moving expanded specifications, comparisons, and secondary-species detail to the supplement. The planned 1–1.5-page subsection must make the reported estimands reproducible; it follows RT01/RT02.


M03 — fuel methods and estimand
Status: Queued — after RT03.
Following RT03, the proposal documents fuel-component definitions, the phase boundary, matched woody contrast, uncertainty/model decisions, and limits on causal interpretation. The planned 1–1.5-page Methods subsection must match the reviewed fuel caption and Results claims, with component/model diagnostics linked through F01 and prediction/inference decisions through RD04.


D01 — regeneration cohort discussion
Status: Queued — after regeneration Results/Methods.
The proposed 1.5–2-page discussion interprets redwood and tanoak regeneration under retained overstory as evidence about developing a new cohort in multiaged stands. It tightens the thesis discussion around accepted basal-area/density findings and their uncertainty, with each inference grounded in Results and cited context.


D02 — sprout development discussion
Status: Queued — after sprout Results/Methods.
The proposed sprout discussion connects accepted height patterns to light, retention, and cohort development. Its 1–1.5 pages must explain what the height evidence adds beyond basal area; combining it with D01 depends on whether the reviewed results support one inseparable management message.


D03 — fuels and PCT-management discussion
Status: Queued — after fuel Results/Methods.
The proposed 1.5–2-page discussion connects phase-specific fuel conditions and the matched woody contrast to silvicultural, fuels, and fire-management questions. It must distinguish potential surface-fuel contribution from directly measured slash and keep interpretation within the reviewed design.


D04 — limits, integration, and future work
Status: Queued.
The proposed closing Discussion subsection integrates the limitations governing regeneration and fuel interpretation, then identifies targeted future work. Its 0.5–1-page allocation is intended to resolve caveats from the topical discussions without repeating detailed model results.


I01 — management problem and study purpose
Status: Queued — after Discussion.
After Discussion, the proposal condenses the multiaged-silviculture framing into the management problem, study purpose, and scope supported by accepted findings.


I02 — regeneration and retention context
Status: Queued — after Discussion.
After Discussion, the proposal retains the sprouting, light, and retention background needed to motivate D01/D02, removing broader context that does not serve the study question.


I03 — fuels context and questions
Status: Queued — after Discussion.
The proposal focuses fuel background on phase-specific reference conditions and the PCT question, excluding broad fire-management claims unsupported by the study. Together I01–I03 target a 4–5-page Introduction whose final questions are answered by accepted Results.


S01 — supplement and machine-readable outputs
Status: Queued — after main displays.
The proposed inventory covers material excluded from the main text: model registries, diagnostics, pairwise comparisons, optional Douglas-fir detail, expanded fuel components, and machine-readable phase values. Each retained item is to be linked from its accepted main-text counterpart after the main displays are reviewed.


C01 — conclusions
Status: Queued — after Discussion.
After Discussion, the proposal is to write a short conclusion restricted to management implications directly supported by the accepted regeneration, sprout, and fuel results.


A01 — abstract and title
Status: Queued — last.
The proposal drafts the abstract from the accepted Results, Methods, Discussion, and Conclusions, then sets the final title after the abstract stabilizes. This is the last task in the backwards-writing sequence.

title: Development workflow
text: This overview describes the publication-development process. The task register and task list summarize the work, and each task has a dedicated review page. Each task is tracked like a small issue: it begins with an objective and guardrails, records the decisions and artifacts produced while it is open, and ends either in a reviewable manuscript product or a completed analytical record. The manuscript is developed backwards from the results displays: figures and tables → results → methods → discussion → introduction → abstract → title. This order adapts the “write backwards” approach described by Montagnes, Montagnes, and Yang (2022).

title: Development workflow
text:
How to use this queue
Each dedicated task page preserves its proposal and detailed review record. Review and edit that proposal, then move the task through this sequence:
Direction for review → Approved to execute → In progress → Pending review → Accepted (or Revision requested) → Complete.
“Queued” means the task is deliberately decomposed and ready to be proposed; it is not yet authorized for execution. “Completed — analytical record” means the reproducible work is preserved, while a decision explicitly marked provisional still awaits scientific review. Page targets are working allocations for the main manuscript, not a journal requirement.

title: Development workflow

The task register and task list are the current planning view. The register links to the task entries below it. Keeping task records current
When work changes, update its dedicated task page first, then revise its entry in publication/tasks.json with a concise summary of that record, its current status, and exact repository file paths. Then render the publication. The pre-render step regenerates the register and summaries, refreshes linked file downloads, and fails if a referenced repository file has moved or disappeared. The manuscript section pages and full draft both include publication/sections/ sources. Edit those shared files once to update both reading views. Review decisions continue to follow the workflow above.

title: Development workflow
text:
Documentation responsibilities
The fuel pipeline map connects the complete analytical and writing sequence. Each step’s QMD and its included review sections own the detailed record: purpose/scope, inputs/dependencies, analyses performed, outputs/findings, decisions/rationale, implications/handoff, and review state/history. Update the originating step when its analysis or decision changes; downstream steps link to that record and explain their own use of it.
F01 owns fuel derivation, exploration, candidate fitting, and provisional model leaders. RD04 owns prediction/inference, uncertainty, the figure/estimates, and retired display history. RT03 owns the Results claims and qualifications. M03 and D03 will own manuscript Methods wording and management interpretation when their queued work begins. Consuming an upstream artifact does not transfer its ownership or accept its provisional scientific decisions.
For the developed fuel records, tasks.json separates produced outputs from consumed inputs and lists depends_on task IDs. File lists and the pipeline map provide navigation; analytical explanations remain on their owning pages. Task summaries are concise descriptions of those records, not another decision log. The pipeline README supplies operational commands and links back to the step documentation.
A continuous pipeline review is not maintained. If it becomes useful for code-agent work, assemble it with Quarto includes of the same step-owned sections. See the maintenance guide for file roles, include conventions, and ownership checks.

title: F01 — fuel-component separation and model exploration
text:
Original objective and guardrails
Create publication-only fuel components that preserve the thesis analyses while making the pre- and post-PCT data usable as distinct reference phases. Retain the fixed experimental-design random-intercept structure; record every model candidate and diagnostic; do not treat an AIC leader as a selected model.

Thesis notebooks, raw data, and thesis-era .rda objects remain unchanged.
Pre-PCT litter and duff are separated using the Finney–Martin model-3 forest-floor partition; post-PCT litter and duff are deliberately omitted because their boundary is not currently defensible.
Woody and herbaceous vegetation are separate in both phases.
The primary PCT contrast is matched-transect pre-PCT minus post-PCT woody standing vegetation—an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not a direct slash-load measurement.
crumbs: F01 — fuel-component separation and model exploration

title: F01 — fuel-component separation and model exploration
text:
Inputs and analyses performed
Stages 01–05 run from analysis/ and write only beneath analysis/outputs/publication/fuel/. The read-only analysis/summarize_collected_data.rda supplies collected measurements. analysis/calculate_fuel_load.rda supplies the unchanged 1-, 10-, 100-, and 1,000-hour components; its combined forest-floor and vegetation columns are not used for the separated components.
Stage 01 derives component loads and audits transect pairing. The pre-PCT forest-floor partition uses Finney and Martin (1993), model 3, with recorded total depth and estimated litter percentage. Negative shallow-extrapolation values are bounded at zero and retained in the station-level audit. Fuel-bed depth is retained for later protocol-comparability review and is not yet interpreted as slash depth. Station and transect data are saved under data/ as .rds files; the downloadable dictionary and pairing CSV describe them.
Stage 02 reports zeros and spread by component and proposes zero and dispersion candidates without fitting models. The design fixes random intercepts for site, site-by-treatment block, and corner nested within block. Stages 03–04 fit the phase-component and matched woody candidates. Each attempted fit records its formula, family, zero/dispersion formulas, warnings, AIC, and DHARMa tests. Stage 05 compares candidates and records provisional AIC leaders. Saved fitted models and registries are the handoff to RD04, not a final scientific selection.

# Publication-only fuel-analysis configuration.
#
# Run the numbered scripts from the analysis/ directory. All publication
# outputs are written beneath analysis/outputs/publication/fuel/; the thesis
# pipeline and its generated objects are read-only inputs.

publication_fuel_paths <- function(analysis_root) {
  list(
    input = file.path(analysis_root, "summarize_collected_data.rda"),
    legacy_load_input = file.path(analysis_root, "calculate_fuel_load.rda"),
    output = file.path(analysis_root, "outputs", "publication", "fuel"),
    data = file.path(analysis_root, "outputs", "publication", "fuel", "data"),
    manifests = file.path(
      analysis_root,
      "outputs",
      "publication",
      "fuel",
      "manifests"
    )
  )
}

publication_fuel_ids <- c("site", "treatment", "corner", "azi")

# Finney and Martin (1993), model 3: cumulative forest-floor mass (Mg ha^-1)
# from the surface to depth ds_cm within a profile of total depth dp_cm.
# The model is used only for the pre-PCT forest-floor measurements, where the
# recorded total depth and estimated litter proportion describe the forest floor.
# Its fitted range does not support a negative cumulative mass; the derivation
# script records and bounds such rare shallow-layer extrapolations at zero.
finney_martin_cumulative_load <- function(ds_cm, dp_cm) {
  result <- 6.461 * ds_cm^1.07 - 0.254 * dp_cm
  result[ds_cm == 0] <- 0
  result
}

fit_component_candidates <- function(data, phase_value, component_value) {
  model_data <- data |>
    filter(
      .data$phase == .env$phase_value,
      .data$component == .env$component_value,
      !is.na(load_mgha)
    )
  zero_count <- sum(model_data$load_mgha == 0)
  prefix <- paste(phase_value, component_value, sep = "_")

  candidates <- list()
  if (zero_count > 0) {
    candidates[["base"]] <- list(glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)", ~1, "~1", ~1, "~1")
    candidates[["disp_treatment"]] <- list(glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)", ~1, "~1", ~treatment, "~treatment")
    if (zero_count >= 8) {
      candidates[["zi_treatment"]] <- list(glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)", ~treatment, "~treatment", ~1, "~1")
    }
  } else {
    candidates[["base"]] <- list(Gamma(link = "log"), "Gamma(link = log)", ~0, "~0", ~1, "~1")
    candidates[["disp_treatment"]] <- list(Gamma(link = "log"), "Gamma(link = log)", ~0, "~0", ~treatment, "~treatment")
  }

  # The thesis used site plus treatment in both the zero and dispersion
  # submodels for post-PCT 100-hour fuels. Retain that candidate and add one
  # deliberately more complex site-by-treatment dispersion sensitivity check.
  if (phase_value == "postpct" && component_value == "hundhr") {
    candidates[["zi_treatment_site_disp_treatment_site"]] <- list(
      glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)",
      ~treatment + site, "~treatment + site",
      ~treatment + site, "~treatment + site"
    )
    candidates[["zi_treatment_site_disp_treatment_site_interaction"]] <- list(
      glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)",
      ~treatment + site, "~treatment + site",
      ~treatment * site, "~treatment * site"
    )
  }

  imap_dfr(candidates, function(candidate, candidate_name) {
    fit_and_diagnose(
      model_id = paste(prefix, candidate_name, sep = "_"),
      response = component_value,
      analysis = paste(phase_value, "phase-specific component", sep = ": "),
      data = model_data,
      formula = design_formula,
      family = candidate[[1]],
      family_label = candidate[[2]],
      ziformula = candidate[[3]],
      ziformula_label = candidate[[4]],
      dispformula = candidate[[5]],
      dispformula_label = candidate[[6]],
      paths = paths
    )
  })
}

  distinct(phase, component) |>
  arrange(phase, component) |>

# Publication-local model fitting and diagnostic helpers.

model_output_paths <- function(paths) {
  models <- file.path(paths$output, "models")
  diagnostics <- file.path(paths$output, "diagnostics")
  dir.create(models, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  dir.create(diagnostics, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  list(models = models, diagnostics = diagnostics)
}

extract_test <- function(test_fun, simulation) {
  result <- tryCatch(test_fun(simulation), error = function(error) error)
  if (inherits(result, "error")) {
    return(list(statistic = NA_real_, p_value = NA_real_, error = conditionMessage(result)))
  }
  list(
    statistic = unname(result$statistic)[1],
    p_value = result$p.value,
    error = NA_character_
  )
}

fit_and_diagnose <- function(
    model_id,
    response,
    analysis,
    data,
    formula,
    family,
    family_label,
    ziformula,
    ziformula_label,
    dispformula,
    dispformula_label,
    paths) {
  output_paths <- model_output_paths(paths)
  warnings <- character()
  fit <- tryCatch(
    withCallingHandlers(
      glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
        formula = formula,
        data = data,
        family = family,
        ziformula = ziformula,
        dispformula = dispformula
      ),
      warning = function(warning) {
        warnings <<- c(warnings, conditionMessage(warning))
        invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
      }
    ),
    error = function(error) error
  )

  base_record <- tibble::tibble(
    model_id = model_id,
    response = response,
    analysis = analysis,
    n = nrow(data),
    fixed_and_random_formula = paste(deparse(formula), collapse = " "),
    family = family_label,
    ziformula = ziformula_label,
    dispformula = dispformula_label,
    fit_status = if (inherits(fit, "error")) "error" else "fit",
    fit_message = if (inherits(fit, "error")) conditionMessage(fit) else NA_character_,
    warnings = if (length(warnings)) paste(unique(warnings), collapse = " | ") else NA_character_,
    pd_hessian = NA,
    aic = NA_real_,
    dharma_uniformity_p = NA_real_,
    dharma_dispersion_p = NA_real_,
    dharma_outlier_p = NA_real_,
    dharma_zero_inflation_p = NA_real_,
    diagnostic_message = NA_character_
  )

  if (inherits(fit, "error")) {
    return(base_record)
  }

  saveRDS(fit, file.path(output_paths$models, paste0(model_id, ".rds")))
  simulation <- tryCatch(
    DHARMa::simulateResiduals(fit, n = 1000, seed = 20260918),
    error = function(error) error
  )
  if (inherits(simulation, "error")) {
    return(dplyr::mutate(
      base_record,
      pd_hessian = fit$sdr$pdHess,
      aic = stats::AIC(fit),
      diagnostic_message = conditionMessage(simulation)
    ))
  }

  # Some DHARMa tests may draw internally. Use a null device so these
  # exploratory diagnostics never create an incidental Rplots.pdf in analysis/.
  grDevices::pdf(file = NULL)
  on.exit(grDevices::dev.off(), add = TRUE)
  uniformity <- extract_test(DHARMa::testUniformity, simulation)
  dispersion <- extract_test(DHARMa::testDispersion, simulation)
  outliers <- extract_test(DHARMa::testOutliers, simulation)
  zero_inflation <- extract_test(DHARMa::testZeroInflation, simulation)

  png(
    filename = file.path(output_paths$diagnostics, paste0(model_id, "-dharma.png")),
    width = 1800,
    height = 900,
    res = 150
  )
  plot(simulation)
  dev.off()

  dplyr::mutate(
    base_record,
    pd_hessian = fit$sdr$pdHess,
    aic = stats::AIC(fit),
    dharma_uniformity_p = uniformity$p_value,
    dharma_dispersion_p = dispersion$p_value,
    dharma_outlier_p = outliers$p_value,
    dharma_zero_inflation_p = zero_inflation$p_value,
    diagnostic_message = paste(
      stats::na.omit(c(uniformity$error, dispersion$error, outliers$error, zero_inflation$error)),
      collapse = " | "
    )
  )
}

# Collate candidate results. This script does not automatically select a final
# model: AIC leaders remain pending DHARMa and scientific review.

script_argument <- grep("^--file=", commandArgs(trailingOnly = FALSE), value = TRUE)
if (length(script_argument) != 1L) stop("Run with Rscript scripts/publication/fuel/05-evaluate-and-select-models.R")
script_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(sub("^--file=", "", script_argument)))
analysis_root <- normalizePath(file.path(script_dir, "..", "..", ".."))
source(file.path(script_dir, "00-fuel-config.R"))

library(dplyr)
library(readr)

paths <- publication_fuel_paths(analysis_root)
registry_files <- c(
  file.path(paths$manifests, "phase-component-model-registry.csv"),
  file.path(paths$manifests, "woody-pct-model-registry.csv")
)
if (!all(file.exists(registry_files))) {
  stop("Run 03-fit-phase-components.R and 04-fit-woody-pct-models.R first.")
}

registry <- bind_rows(lapply(registry_files, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)) |>
  mutate(
    comparison_group = paste(response, analysis, sep = " | ")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    aic_rank = if_else(fit_status == "fit", rank(aic, ties.method = "min"), NA_real_),
    delta_aic = if_else(
      fit_status == "fit",
      aic - min(aic[fit_status == "fit"], na.rm = TRUE),
      NA_real_
    ),
    .by = comparison_group
  ) |>
  arrange(comparison_group, aic_rank, model_id)

selection_log <- registry |>
  filter(fit_status == "fit", aic_rank == 1) |>
  mutate(
    diagnostic_follow_up = rowSums(
      across(starts_with("dharma_"), ~ !is.na(.x) & .x < 0.05)
    ) > 0
  ) |>
  transmute(
    response,
    analysis,
    provisional_aic_leader = model_id,
    aic,
    pd_hessian,
    dharma_uniformity_p,
    dharma_dispersion_p,
    dharma_outlier_p,
    dharma_zero_inflation_p,
    selection_status = case_when(
      !pd_hessian ~ "rejected pending convergence resolution",
      diagnostic_follow_up ~ "requires diagnostic follow-up",
      TRUE ~ "eligible for scientific review"
    ),
    selection_rationale = "This is the AIC-leading predeclared candidate, not a final selection. Retain only after diagnostic and scientific review."
  )

write_csv(registry, file.path(paths$manifests, "model-comparison.csv"))
write_csv(selection_log, file.path(paths$manifests, "model-selection-log.csv"))

title: RD02 — regeneration basal-area/density display
text:
Status: Separate models selected; displays pending review. Working target: RW/TO Results figure and all-species supplement table.
Redwood, tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species are each modeled with ba_ha ~ treat + (1 | site/treat), using zero-inflated Gamma responses and category-specific zero and dispersion intercepts. The choice follows the biological interpretation of separate species responses and variances. There are four sites, 16 macro plots, and 64 vegetation-plot observations per category; no plot-level random effect is included.

title: RD02 — regeneration basal-area/density display
text:
Selected display and supplement








Figure 1: Regeneration basal area 10 years after harvest by retained-overstory treatment. Points are arithmetic expected basal area, including modeled zeros and integrated over fitted site and nested macro-plot random intercepts; colored ranges are 95% confidence intervals for the means from the full-parameter log-scale delta method. Blue ranges with circles denote redwood and orange ranges with triangles denote tanoak. Each species is modeled separately using zero-inflated Gamma responses with treatment as a fixed effect and four site and 16 nested macro-plot random intercepts, using 64 vegetation-plot observations per species. GS = group selection; LD = low-density dispersed retention; HA = high-density aggregated retention; HD = high-density dispersed retention. Species panels use different vertical scales. Intervals describe uncertainty in means, not new-plot variation or pairwise significance tests.





The RW/TO display is in the Results body, and all 16 species-by-treatment means and intervals are in the supplement table. Means include zeros and integrate over fitted site and macro-plot random effects. The earlier joint fit is retained in the comparison record below.

title: RD02 — regeneration basal-area/density display
text:
Overall model sensitivity
Comparison record. The comparison includes three joint structures—site by species, full design nesting, and both together—fitted to all four species (256 rows) and to RW/TO only (128 rows). Separate RW and TO fits use site and macro-plot random intercepts, with the plot-level effect omitted. The selected four-category separate models are included in the 256-row comparison. AIC ranks models within each dataset; the separate pair combines both species’ likelihoods and parameter counts.




Table 1: Sensitivity-model fit. Delta AIC is calculated within each dataset. Separate-species rows combine independent category likelihoods and parameter counts: 32 parameters for four categories, 16 for RW/TO. The selected primary analysis is marked. All component fits converged with positive-definite Hessians.

Figure 2: Overall basal-area sensitivity. Top panels show joint fits and the selected separate models for all four categories; bottom panels show RW/TO joint fits and separate species models with site and macro-plot random intercepts. Points are arithmetic means including modeled zeros and integrated over fitted random effects; ranges are approximate 95% confidence intervals from the full-covariance log-scale delta method. Vertical scales differ between panels.





Notable patterns across the comparisons:

Treatment patterns persist. Redwood means follow GS > LD > HA > HD; tanoak means follow GS > LD > HD > HA. The redwood–tanoak ranking within HD changes under shared full nesting, so that species comparison is sensitive to model structure.
Separate species show different site variation. Site SDs are about 0.72 for RW and 0.16 for TO; macro-plot variances approach zero. RW has a wider GS interval, while TO intervals are narrower than in the lead draft. Removing the plot-level effect leaves means and intervals unchanged at two decimals and lowers the separate pair’s AIC by 4.00 to 508.78, slightly below joint full nesting (509.53). Site-by-species remains lowest within both datasets.
Diagnostics are broadly consistent. Uniformity, dispersion, and zero-frequency checks show no flags across models. Only the four-species thesis fit has an outlier flag: p = 0.015 with 1,000 simulations and about 0.050 with 10,000, with different observations flagged. The RW/TO refits and separate models show no outlier flags. Alternative-optimizer checks agree.



Data and reproducible code

Fit comparisons, means and intervals, variance components, diagnostic tests, figure PDF, assembly code, input checksums, and provenance. The fitting scripts are available for the joint comparison and separate-species comparison.

title: RD02 — regeneration basal-area/density display
text:
Separate RW and TO models
Each species uses ba_ha ~ treat + (1 | site/treat): site and nested macro-plot intercepts, zero-inflated Gamma responses, and species-specific zero and dispersion intercepts. The plot-level random effect is omitted.
The focused comparison shows the main difference: separate fitting increases RW’s GS mean and uncertainty, while TO changes less. Separate-model GS means are 12.66 (3.67, 43.72) for RW and 2.21 (1.38, 3.55) m² ha⁻¹ for TO (mean and 95% CI).








Figure 3: Focused species-model sensitivity: the earlier joint four-species fit, joint RW/TO full nesting, and separate species fits with site and macro-plot random intercepts. Points are random-effect-integrated means including zeros; ranges are approximate 95% confidence intervals. Vertical scales differ between species.

title: RD02 — regeneration basal-area/density display
text:
Summary and model decision
Selected approach. Fit redwood, tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species separately with treatment as a fixed effect and site and nested macro-plot random intercepts. This choice prioritizes biological interpretation and species-specific variance estimation. The RW/TO figure is in the Results; all-category values are in the supplement. The joint-model comparisons remain as sensitivity evidence.
All four selected fits converge with positive-definite Hessians and no flags in the overall residual checks. Macro-plot variances approach zero; site variation differs substantially among categories, with Douglas-fir also near zero. Means include zeros and integrate over both random effects. Four sites still limit variance precision; interval stability remains a useful bootstrap check before final inferential claims.


Selected-model source and diagnostics

The publication-only pipeline fits four separate categories from the saved regeneration data. All 16 means pass prediction, gradient, and integration checks; the RW/TO estimates reproduce the separate-species sensitivity fits. Thesis files and earlier joint-model artifacts remain unchanged.
Estimates, fit register, diagnostics, variance components, optimizer checks, generator, provenance, and figure PDF.

text:

This page owns fuel prediction and inference decisions, the figure and companion table, their source/output review, and the history of replaced display code. See the fuel pipeline map for the complete sequence.
The figure has been generated from the current AIC-leading fitted publication models. Its position in the register is an organizational sequence, not a required execution order relative to RD02 or RD03.

Produce a compact, reviewable full-inventory figure (and caption) from the current AIC-leading fitted publication models. title: RD04 — fuel phase and PCT display
text:
Prediction and interpretation review
Implemented approach: use study-standardized, population-averaged expected loads as the baseline for mean fuel loading in comparable systems. Integrate over the fitted random-intercept distributions and include modeled zeros, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts. Retain the historical zero-random-effect predictions as a clearly labeled reference/sensitivity summary in the audit. RD04 now uses this integrated interpretation throughout, with woody mean change derived from the joint phase model; the fitted load models remain provisional pending scientific review. The original generator has been retired in favor of 08-generate-rd04-integrated-figure.R.

What the prediction arguments actually do








Calculation
Quantity estimated
Appropriate interpretation




re.form = NULL with known grouping IDs
Expected response conditional on fitted random effects for those sites, blocks, corners, and transects
Conditions in the sampled units; average over an explicitly weighted set of these units if that is the target


re.form = NA (or ~0)
Expected response with all random effects set to zero
A reference at the center of the latent random-effect distribution


re.form = NULL, with selected random-only grouping variables set to NA in newdata
Retains known-group effects for the remaining grouping variables and sets the selected groups’ effects to zero
A conditional reference, e.g., a known site with zero lower-level effects


Integrate expected responses over the fitted random-effect distribution
Arithmetic expected load for a population of exchangeable sampling units
The model-based mean-load baseline used in RD04



marginaleffects passes the random-effect arguments to the fitted model’s prediction method. Its by argument and avg_predictions() average the predictions supplied to them; they do not change zero-effect predictions into random-effect-integrated predictions. This distinction follows the mixed-model vignette, the prediction reference, and the distinction between observed-group averaging and new-group integration in the Bayesian vignette.
For glmmTMB, arbitrary formulas selecting random effects in re.form are not supported. Selected grouping variables can instead be set to NA, but this is unsuitable when a variable is also required as a fixed predictor: site, for example, must remain defined for the post-PCT 100-hour model’s zero component. allow.new.levels = TRUE permits new grouping IDs; it does not request integration over their possible effects. See the model’s prediction documentation.
Two different uses of “conditional” also need separating: type = "conditional" requests the conditional-distribution mean, whereas re.form controls conditioning on random effects. For these zero-inflated Gamma models, type = "response" returns \((1-p_0)\mu_+\), including the modeled probability of zero, while type = "conditional" returns \(\mu_+\). Dispersion parameters affect variability and estimation but are not additional multipliers of this response mean. Gamma sampling variability should not receive a lognormal residual-variance correction.


Alignment of the thesis code and interpretation
The controlling Results function is marginaleffects_to_emmeans() in analysis/thesis/results.qmd: both predictions and comparisons use re.form = NA. For fuel loads, its pre- and post-PCT calls use tidyr::expand(data, treatment, site), giving equal site weights. Passing the predictions and pairwise-difference standard errors into emmeans::emmobj() changes their representation, not their underlying estimand. The earlier re.form = NULL exploratory basal-area plots in regen_visualize.qmd are not the calls controlling the thesis Results.







Thesis statement or presentation
Assessment




Methods: predictions incorporate all components and average over random effects to obtain population means
Partly aligned: response predictions can include the zero component, but the wrapper sets random effects to zero before averaging. The random effects were not integrated out.


Methods: estimates apply to equal proportions of similar sites, specifically north- and south-facing aspects
Equal site weights are explicit for fuel grids. Zeroing site random effects does not reproduce an aspect mixture on a nonlinear response scale; aspect was not a fixed adjustment variable. Transport requires an exchangeability assumption beyond the prediction settings.


Fuel Results: “expected value” and “estimated marginal means”
Valid if identified as site-standardized expectations at zero random effects. Too broad if read as arithmetic population-average loads across forest heterogeneity.


Discussion: compare “average” loads with other forest studies
State whether each value is an observed mean, a zero-effect reference, or an integrated model mean, and check component definitions and sampling protocols. These quantities are not interchangeable.


Post-PCT caption: vegetation difference “represents slash fuels recruited to the forest floor”
Overstates the measurement: standing-vegetation reduction is an inferred potential contribution, not measured slash deposition. RD04’s qualified caption is better aligned.


Results: pre/post estimates are not statistically comparable because model structures differ
Different structures alone do not prevent comparison. Formal phase differences need an explicit common estimand and their covariance, accounting for pairing. Separate phase CIs do not supply a paired change test.


Discussion/conclusions: PCT “resulted in” or “generated” the observed dead-fuel changes
The observed transition supports association; attributing all change to PCT requires the design/time assumptions. No unthinned contemporaneous comparison is used by these predictions.



The same wrapper controls regeneration and sprout Results. Basal area, Douglas-fir counts, and year-10 height use nonlinear links, so zero-effect and integrated means can differ there too. Height increment uses an identity link; integration over mean-zero random effects leaves its expected value unchanged, for a fixed covariate distribution. The Results grids also vary: treatment height-increment summaries explicitly balance years, whereas the by-year analysis uses newdata = NULL and averages within observed species/year cells. Those are different standardization choices and should be described separately. The fuel integration code below is deliberately restricted to its audited model structures; it is not a general-purpose replacement for those other analyses.
One numerical provenance issue also deserves attention: the Discussion reports about 42 Mg/ha of pre-PCT 1,000-hour fuel. Reproducing the Results wrapper on the saved thesis models gives an equal-treatment reference mean of 32.63 Mg/ha. The Discussion value may be an observed summary, but it should not be presented as the grand mean of these particular model predictions without a separate source. The audit preserves all reproduced thesis fuel estimates.


How RD04 compares with the thesis
The original RD04 and thesis fuel Results used the same zero-random-effect target and equal-site weighting. Both used valid prediction grids: the thesis expanded the observed treatment and site levels, and RD04 retained observed rows with valid nested identifiers, one per site/treatment/phase. Neither approach introduced a grid discrepancy for these zero-effect predictions. The updated RD04 retains equal-site weighting and integrates over random effects. Every phase-specific mean averages four site contexts; post-PCT 100-hour fuel additionally retains fixed site effects in its zero component.
Numerical changes from the thesis to the original RD04 arose from revised fitted models and component definitions, not a switch from marginaleffects to custom prediction. The updated figure also changes the estimand by integrating over random effects. The directly comparable deadwood example below separates these changes. Values are Mg/ha, GS treatment.

Implemented target and worked demonstration
For a treatment \(t\), phase \(h\), and equally weighted site contexts \(s\), define
\[
M_{th} = \frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4}
  E_b\!\left[(1-p_{0,sth})\exp\{x_{sth}^{\mathsf T}\beta + z^{\mathsf T}b\}\right].
\]
The audited load models have independent Gaussian random intercepts only in the conditional model and no random effects in the zero component. Thus, with \(v=\sum_k\sigma_k^2\) across all modeled random-intercept levels,
\[
M_{th}=\exp(v/2)\,
\frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4}(1-p_{0,sth})\exp(x_{sth}^{\mathsf T}\beta).
\]
This is exact under the fitted model, not a generic bias-correction option. The same multiplier across treatments within a fitted load model preserves ratios and rankings, while changing absolute loads and differences. Inference must still propagate uncertainty in the multiplier; old p-values and standard errors should not simply be carried over.
The separate Student-t difference model was replaced in the display by the integrated joint phase-model contrast so that woody change equals the difference between the displayed arithmetic mean loads. Its uncertainty retains the joint pre/post covariance, keeping the change estimate consistent with the matched design and the mean-load interpretation of the other panels.
For post-PCT 100-hour fuel, “site-standardized” specifically retains an equal mixture of the four fitted zero-process site contexts. Integration of the random intercepts cannot create a zero-process coefficient for a fifth site. The baseline therefore concerns comparable contexts, not a fitted prediction for any arbitrary new forest. Four sites also provide limited information about the site-variance distribution. A regional mean, or an explicitly 50:50 aspect-standardized mean, would need a justified target distribution and sufficient covariate information to support that standardization.
The demonstration holds fitted load models fixed and changes the estimand; woody change now uses their joint phase model. Selected GS examples below show why the distinction matters (Mg/ha). The intervals describe uncertainty in the integrated mean, not variation in a new forest or transect.

The implementation in 07-audit-rd04-inference.R demonstrates both routes:

Historical reference target: marginaleffects::avg_predictions(model, newdata = grid, by = ..., type = "response", re.form = NA) agrees with predict() followed by explicit matrix averaging. The custom variance is A %*% prediction$cov.fit %*% t(A).
Implemented integrated target: a nonlinear functional supplied to marginaleffects::hypotheses() averages the response means after analytic integration. A separate custom implementation derives its gradient and calculates G %*% V %*% t(G). Both use the full covariance of the fitted nonrandom parameters, including zero-model coefficients, log random-effect standard deviations, and their cross-covariances. Merely multiplying an avg_predictions() interval by exp(v/2) would omit uncertainty in \(v\).

The hypotheses documentation supports nonlinear functionals and supplied covariance matrices. Here the full parameter table is supplied explicitly because ordinary fixed-coefficient prediction covariance alone does not include the integration multiplier’s variance. These are asymptotic delta-method intervals, conditional on the chosen models and the reference grid. They do not include model-selection or fuel-component-derivation uncertainty. Refitted parametric bootstrap intervals are a useful final sensitivity check, particularly for herbaceous loads with large variance corrections and only four sites.
Verification: the audit checks all 60 historical comparison cells for agreement of reference point estimates and SEs, integrated point estimates, and integrated SEs; the latter agree within a relative/absolute tolerance of \(10^{-4}\). It checks the integration multiplier against numerical quadrature, the matrix predictions against predict.glmmTMB(), and the retired script’s checksum before and after the run. It additionally verifies all four woody mean contrasts with cross-phase covariance and reproduces the 48 thesis fuel reference estimates. Outputs and the R/package session record are in analysis/outputs/publication/fuel/inference-audit/.
Review the complete audit and inference-helper source.


Methods wording
For the implemented population-average baseline:

We estimated treatment- and phase-specific mean fuel loads by averaging response-scale expectations, including modeled zeros, over an equally weighted grid of the four study-site contexts and analytically integrating over all fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances.

The matched-contrast qualification can be stated in its own Methods sentence:

Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

The former figure-and-table plan has been merged into this task; this is the authoritative action record for fuel-display development.

section: Inference and display code and outputs
text:
Inference and display code and outputs
This section is the authoritative source review for RD04 prediction, inference, and display implementation. It reads the original scripts and saved CSVs on every render. The F01 analytical record owns the upstream component derivation and fitted-model candidates; the fuel pipeline map shows their dependencies.

Complete RD04 scripts
Stage 07 audits inference; stage 08 generates the current integrated-mean figure and estimates. Their shared inference functions are included here. Stage 06 and its archived implementation are retained as historical evidence.


06-generate-rd04-figure.R — retired entry point

Download source
# Retired entry point. The historical implementation is retained only for audit.
stop("This generator is retired. Run Rscript scripts/publication/fuel/08-generate-rd04-integrated-figure.R from analysis/ instead.", call. = FALSE)




07-audit-rd04-inference.R

Download source
# Read-only audit of the fitted RD04 models and thesis fuel predictions.
# Run from analysis/: Rscript scripts/publication/fuel/07-audit-rd04-inference.R
# Historical zero-effect estimates are read from the retired generator.
script_argument <- grep("^--file=", commandArgs(FALSE), value = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(script_argument) == 1L)
script_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(sub("^--file=", "", script_argument)))
analysis_root <- normalizePath(file.path(script_dir, "..", "..", ".."))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(glmmTMB)
  library(marginaleffects)
  library(readr)
  library(tidyr)
})
models_dir <- file.path(analysis_root, "outputs/publication/fuel/models")
audit_dir <- file.path(analysis_root, "outputs/publication/fuel/inference-audit")
dir.create(audit_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Evaluate only these two definitions, never the original script's output steps.
original_script <- file.path(script_dir, "retired", "06-generate-rd04-figure.R")
original_hash <- tools::md5sum(original_script)
for (expr in parse(original_script)) {
  if (is.call(expr) && identical(expr[[1]], as.name("<-")) && is.symbol(expr[[2]]) &&
      as.character(expr[[2]]) %in% c("model_ids", "model_estimates")) eval(expr)
}

source(file.path(script_dir, "rd04-inference-utils.R"))

spec <- tibble(
  key = names(model_ids), model_id = unname(model_ids),
  component = c("1-hour", "1-hour", "10-hour", "10-hour", "100-hour", "100-hour",
                "1,000-hour", "1,000-hour", "Woody vegetation", "Herbaceous vegetation",
                "Herbaceous vegetation", "Litter", "Duff", "Woody difference"),
  phase = c(rep(c("prepct", "postpct"), 4), NA, "prepct", "postpct", "prepct", "prepct", NA)
)
spec <- bind_rows(filter(spec, key != "woody_phase"),
                  mutate(filter(spec, key == "woody_phase"), phase = "prepct"),
                  mutate(filter(spec, key == "woody_phase"), phase = "postpct"))

audit <- list()
structures <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(spec))) {
  item <- spec[i, ]
  message("Auditing ", item$model_id, " ", item$phase)
  model <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, paste0(item$model_id, ".rds")))
  phase_arg <- if (is.na(item$phase)) NULL else item$phase
  grid <- reference_grid(model, phase_arg)
  avg <- averaging_matrix(grid)
  reference <- custom_reference(model, grid)
  me <- as.data.frame(avg_predictions(model, newdata = grid, type = "response",
                       by = intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(grid)),
                       re.form = NA, allow.new.levels = TRUE))
  me <- me[match(as.character(reference$treatment), as.character(me$treatment)), ]
  legacy <- model_estimates(item$model_id, item$component, phase_arg,
                            difference = item$key == "woody_difference")
  legacy <- legacy[match(as.character(reference$treatment), as.character(legacy$treatment)), ]
  s <- integration_setup(model, grid)
  integrated <- custom_integrated(s)
  me_integrated <- as.data.frame(marginaleffects_integrated(s))
  stopifnot(max(abs(reference$estimate - me$estimate)) < 1e-6,
            max(abs(reference$std.error - me$std.error) / pmax(1, reference$std.error)) < 1e-4,
            max(abs(reference$estimate - legacy$estimate)) < 1e-6,
            max(abs(integrated$estimate - me_integrated$estimate)) < 1e-6,
            max(abs(integrated$se - me_integrated$std.error) / pmax(1, integrated$se)) < 1e-4)
  # Verify integration at a point using numerical quadrature, independently of
  # the closed-form exp(v/2) calculation (including near-zero variances).
  if (s$link == "log") {
    quadrature <- integrate(function(z) exp(sqrt(s$variance) * z) * dnorm(z),
                            lower = -12, upper = 12, rel.tol = 1e-9)$value
    stopifnot(abs(quadrature - exp(s$variance / 2)) < 1e-7)
  }
  # Check matrix construction against the model's own predict implementation.
  row0 <- if (s$link == "log") exp(drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib])) else drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib])
  if (length(s$iz)) row0 <- row0 * (1 - plogis(drop(s$Z %*% s$par[s$iz])))
  stopifnot(max(abs(row0 - predict(model, grid, type = "response", re.form = NA))) < 1e-6)
  # Average ALL observed rows within site, then equally across sites; retaining
  # only one corner/transect per site would give an arbitrary conditional mean.
  observed <- model$frame
  if (!is.null(phase_arg) && "phase" %in% names(observed)) observed <- filter(observed, .data$phase == .env$phase_arg)
  conditional <- observed |>
    mutate(predicted = as.numeric(predict(model, observed, type = "response", re.form = NULL))) |>
    group_by(across(all_of(intersect(c("site", "treatment", "phase"), names(observed))))) |>
    summarise(predicted = mean(predicted), .groups = "drop") |>
    group_by(across(all_of(intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(observed))))) |>
    summarise(predicted = mean(predicted), .groups = "drop")
  fitted_groups <- conditional$predicted[match(as.character(reference$treatment), as.character(conditional$treatment))]
  # Marginal mean intervals: log-delta intervals stay positive without truncation;
  # the signed identity-link difference uses ordinary response-scale intervals.
  lcl <- if (s$link == "log") integrated$estimate * exp(-qnorm(.975) * integrated$se / integrated$estimate) else integrated$estimate - qnorm(.975) * integrated$se
  ucl <- if (s$link == "log") integrated$estimate * exp(qnorm(.975) * integrated$se / integrated$estimate) else integrated$estimate + qnorm(.975) * integrated$se
  audit[[i]] <- tibble(
    model_id = item$model_id, component = item$component, phase = item$phase,
    treatment = as.character(reference$treatment), n_sites = rowSums(avg$A > 0),
    reference_custom = reference$estimate, reference_marginaleffects = me$estimate,
    original_se = legacy$se, corrected_reference_se = reference$std.error,
    marginaleffects_reference_se = me$std.error,
    fitted_group_site_balanced_mean = fitted_groups,
    random_intercept_variance = s$variance,
    integration_multiplier = if (s$link == "log") exp(s$variance / 2) else 1,

summarize_integrated <- function(s, component, model_id, phase = NULL, difference = FALSE) {

  low <- if (difference) prediction$estimate - qnorm(.975) * prediction$se else
    prediction$estimate * exp(-qnorm(.975) * prediction$se / prediction$estimate)

    prediction$estimate * exp(qnorm(.975) * prediction$se / prediction$estimate)

         treatment = as.character(labels$treatment), estimate = prediction$estimate,
         se = prediction$se, lcl = low, ucl = high, model_id = model_id,
         estimand = if (difference) "integrated matched woody mean difference (pre-PCT minus post-PCT)" else
           "site-standardized random-effect-integrated expected load",

# Keep valid nested identifiers from one observed row per site/treatment/phase.
# These identifiers do not contribute fitted random effects when re.form=NA.
reference_grid <- function(model, phase = NULL) {
  keys <- intersect(c("site", "treatment", "phase"), names(model$frame))
  grid <- distinct(model$frame, across(all_of(keys)), .keep_all = TRUE)
  if (!is.null(phase) && "phase" %in% keys) grid <- filter(grid, .data$phase == .env$phase)
  counts <- count(grid, treatment)
  stopifnot(length(unique(counts$n)) == 1L)
  grid
}

# A maps row predictions to equally weighted site means. A V A' retains every
# cross-site covariance; treating site predictions as independent is incorrect.
averaging_matrix <- function(grid) {
  keys <- intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(grid))
  labels <- distinct(grid, across(all_of(keys)))
  A <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(labels)), function(i) {
    keep <- Reduce(`&`, lapply(keys, function(k) grid[[k]] == labels[[k]][i]))
    as.numeric(keep) / sum(keep)
  }, numeric(nrow(grid))))
  list(A = A, labels = labels)
}

custom_reference <- function(model, grid) {
  p <- predict(model, newdata = grid, type = "response", re.form = NA,
               allow.new.levels = TRUE, se.fit = TRUE, cov.fit = TRUE)
  avg <- averaging_matrix(grid)
  transform(avg$labels, estimate = as.vector(avg$A %*% p$fit),
            std.error = sqrt(diag(avg$A %*% p$cov.fit %*% t(avg$A))))
}

# Exact integration for THESE models: independent Gaussian random intercepts in
# the conditional model, log/identity link, no random effects in the zero model.
# This deliberately fails on slopes, correlated effects, offsets, or other links.
integration_setup <- function(model, grid) {
  vc <- VarCorr(model)
  stopifnot(length(vc$zi) == 0L, length(vc$disp) == 0L,
            all(vapply(vc$cond, function(x) identical(dim(x), c(1L, 1L)), logical(1))))
  X <- model.matrix(delete.response(terms(formula(model, fixed.only = TRUE))), grid)
  Z <- model.matrix(formula(model, component = "zi", fixed.only = TRUE), grid)
  par <- model$fit$par
  ib <- which(names(par) == "beta")
  iz <- which(names(par) == "betazi")
  it <- which(names(par) == "theta")
  stopifnot(ncol(X) == length(ib), ncol(Z) == length(iz),
            length(it) == length(vc$cond), model$sdr$pdHess,
            isTRUE(all.equal(unname(par), unname(model$sdr$par.fixed))),
            is.null(model.offset(model$frame)),
            family(model)$link %in% c("log", "identity"))
  variance <- sum(vapply(vc$cond, function(x) x[1, 1], numeric(1)))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(variance, sum(exp(2 * par[it])), tolerance = 1e-8)))
  list(X = X, Z = Z, par = par, V = model$sdr$cov.fixed,
       ib = ib, iz = iz, it = it, link = family(model)$link,
       avg = averaging_matrix(grid), variance = variance)
}

# Independent analytic derivatives for the custom delta-method implementation.
custom_integrated <- function(s) {
  eta <- drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib])
  pzero <- if (length(s$iz)) plogis(drop(s$Z %*% s$par[s$iz])) else rep(0, length(eta))
  if (s$link == "log") {
    mu <- exp(eta + s$variance / 2) * (1 - pzero)
    D <- matrix(0, nrow(s$X), length(s$par))
    D[, s$ib] <- mu * s$X
    if (length(s$iz)) D[, s$iz] <- -mu * pzero * s$Z
    D[, s$it] <- outer(mu, exp(2 * s$par[s$it]))
  } else {
    stopifnot(length(s$iz) == 0L)
    mu <- eta
    D <- matrix(0, nrow(s$X), length(s$par))
    D[, s$ib] <- s$X
  }
  G <- s$avg$A %*% D
  list(estimate = drop(s$avg$A %*% mu),
       se = sqrt(pmax(0, diag(G %*% s$V %*% t(G)))), G = G)
}

# Contrast the same matched model's integrated phase means, retaining their
# covariance through a single gradient and the full parameter covariance.
woody_change_setup <- function(s) {
  labels <- s$avg$labels
  stopifnot(all(c("phase", "treatment") %in% names(labels)),
            setequal(unique(as.character(labels$phase)), c("prepct", "postpct")))
  treatments <- unique(as.character(labels$treatment))
  C <- t(vapply(treatments, function(trt) {
    stopifnot(sum(labels$treatment == trt & labels$phase == "prepct") == 1L,
              sum(labels$treatment == trt & labels$phase == "postpct") == 1L)
    as.numeric(labels$treatment == trt) * ifelse(labels$phase == "prepct", 1, -1)
  }, numeric(nrow(labels))))
  s$avg$A <- C %*% s$avg$A
  s$avg$labels <- data.frame(treatment = treatments)
  s
}

# marginaleffects does the nonlinear delta method on a supplied full parameter
# table, including theta (log SDs), not just the conditional fixed coefficients.
# avg_predictions(re.form=NA) alone does NOT integrate over random effects.
marginaleffects_integrated <- function(s) {
  parameters <- data.frame(term = paste0("p", seq_along(s$par)),
                           estimate = unname(s$par))
  functional <- function(x) {
    b <- x$estimate
    eta <- drop(s$X %*% b[s$ib])
    pzero <- if (length(s$iz)) plogis(drop(s$Z %*% b[s$iz])) else rep(0, length(eta))
    mu <- if (s$link == "log") exp(eta + sum(exp(2 * b[s$it])) / 2) * (1 - pzero) else eta
    data.frame(term = seq_len(nrow(s$avg$labels)), estimate = drop(s$avg$A %*% mu))
  }
  marginaleffects::hypotheses(parameters, hypothesis = functional, vcov = s$V,
             numderiv = "fdcenter", conf_level = .95)
}

    cov.fit = TRUE,
    re.form = NA,
    allow.new.levels = TRUE
  )
  grid <- mutate(grid, estimate_site = as.numeric(prediction$fit))
  group_columns <- intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(grid))
  groups <- grid |>
    mutate(row_id = row_number()) |>
    group_by(across(all_of(group_columns))) |>
    summarise(row_ids = list(row_id), estimate = mean(estimate_site), .groups = "drop")
  groups <- groups |>
    rowwise() |>
    mutate(
      se = sqrt(sum(prediction$cov.fit[row_ids[[1]], row_ids[[1]], drop = FALSE]) / length(row_ids[[1]])^2),
      lcl = estimate - stats::qnorm(0.975) * se,
      ucl = estimate + stats::qnorm(0.975) * se
    ) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(
      component = component,
      model_id = model_id,
      estimand = if (difference) "matched woody vegetation difference (pre-PCT minus post-PCT)" else "phase-specific expected load",
      phase = phase_label,
      lcl = if (difference) lcl else pmax(0, lcl),
      treatment = factor(treatment, levels = c("gs", "ld", "ha", "hd"))
    )
  select(groups, component, phase, treatment, estimate, se, lcl, ucl, model_id, estimand)
}

phase_colors <- c("Pre-PCT" = "#C96F38", "Post-PCT" = "#3F51B5")
phase_position <- position_dodge(width = 0.52)

phase_panel <- function(component_name) {
  data <- filter(estimates, .data$component == .env$component_name)
  ggplot(data, aes(x = treatment, y = estimate, ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl, color = phase, group = phase)) +
    geom_linerange(linewidth = 2.2, position = phase_position) +
    geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "black", size = 2.5, stroke = 0.6, position = phase_position) +
    scale_color_manual(values = phase_colors, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c(gs = "GS", ld = "LD", ha = "HA", hd = "HD")) +
    labs(title = component_name, x = NULL, y = expression(Load ~ (Mg %.% ha^-1))) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}

difference_panel <- function() {
  data <- difference_component
  ggplot(data, aes(x = treatment, y = estimate, ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray45", linewidth = 0.45) +
    geom_linerange(color = "#5A4A42", linewidth = 2.2) +
    geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "black", size = 2.5, stroke = 0.6) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c(gs = "GS", ld = "LD", ha = "HA", hd = "HD")) +
    labs(
      title = "Woody vegetation difference\n(pre-PCT minus post-PCT)",
      x = NULL,
      y = expression(Load ~ difference ~ (Mg %.% ha^-1))
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Forest managers using retention forestry need information on regeneration and fuel development to design productive stands in fire-adapted ecosystems. We analyzed 10-year remeasurement data from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment in Jackson Demonstration State Forest, California. The experiment compared group selection, aggregated retention, and low- and high-density dispersed retention treatments and measured regeneration, sprout growth, and surface fuel loading.
Redwood regeneration responded strongly to increasing canopy openness, whereas tanoak responses were more modest. Sprout-height findings will remain part of the main regeneration evidence. Fuel measurements describe conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including the PCT-associated contrast. The manuscript will evaluate how overstory retention affects regeneration while presenting fuel components in a form useful for integrated silviculture, fuels, and fire management.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Study area and design
The experiment is located in the Jackson Demonstration State Forest in coastal northern California. Four harvest treatments were replicated at four sites in 2012: group selection (GS), high-density dispersed retention (HD), high-density aggregated retention (HA), and low-density dispersed retention (LD). The retained-overstory treatments targeted post-harvest relative densities of 13% or 21%; group selection created a 1-ha opening with a lightly thinned buffer. These treatments were designed to examine alternative pathways for developing multiaged redwood stands (Berrill & O’Hara, 2009; Reineke, 1933).
Ten years after harvest, regeneration plots and fuel transects were established within each 0.2-ha treatment macro plot. Regeneration measurements characterized redwood, tanoak, and Douglas-fir; fuel transects characterized dead surface fuels and live vegetation. The plots were remeasured after precommercial thinning, which released selected conifers from competing trees and shrubs.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Analysis
Detailed sampling procedures, model diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses will be retained as supplementary material.

Regeneration basal area
Basal area was modeled separately for redwood, tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species using zero-inflated Gamma mixed models with a conditional log link. Treatment was a fixed effect; site and macro plot nested within site were random intercepts. Each species category had its own intercept-only zero and dispersion components. Each model used 64 vegetation-plot observations from four sites and 16 macro plots. Arithmetic mean basal area included modeled zeros and integrated over both fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. Confidence intervals for the means were calculated using the log-scale delta method with the full parameter covariance, including random-effect variance uncertainty. Redwood and tanoak estimates are displayed in the Results; estimates for all four categories are reported in the supplement.


Fuel loads and PCT contrast
Reported values are model-based arithmetic mean loads, including modeled zeros and integrating over fitted random effects, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts.
These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
section: Fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning
text:
Fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning

Dead fuel loading
Fuel measurements ten years after harvest characterized conditions before and after precommercial thinning (PCT) across the four retention treatments (Figure 2). Following PCT, group selection (GS) and low-density dispersed retention (LD) showed the largest estimated increases in fine dead-fuel loads and reductions in woody standing vegetation. These treatments also had the highest post-PCT fine dead-fuel loads. Pre-PCT dead-fuel estimates suggested subtler, component-specific treatment patterns. Fuel loads are reported as model-estimated means, with 95% confidence intervals. Woody and herbaceous standing vegetation are reported separately, as are pre-PCT litter and duff. All loads and load differences below are in Mg ha-1.
Before PCT, estimated 1-hour fuel loads were highest in high-density aggregated retention (HA; 1.2) and lowest in GS (0.6), with LD and high-density dispersed (HD) retention intermediate. Estimated 10-hour loads ranged from 2.8 in HD to 3.8 in GS, and 100-hour loads from 9.0 to 11.5 in those same treatments. The 1,000-hour class had larger mean loads, ranging from 30.2 in LD to 49.6 (95% CI 25.9 to 95.0) in GS. Uncertainty was substantial for this coarse-wood component across treatments.
The separated forest-floor components showed different treatment patterns. Pre-PCT litter estimates ranged from 12.6 in LD to 18.4 in GS; HA and HD were intermediate. Duff estimates were lowest in HA, at 19.3 (95% CI 14.5 to 25.8), and highest in HD, at 35.5 (95% CI 26.6 to 47.4), with GS and LD both near 28–29. These are model-derived forest-floor loads based on the estimated litter-depth boundary. Post-PCT litter and duff were not estimated because the forest-floor boundary could not be distinguished reliably in the presence of slash and suspended foliage.
After PCT, estimated 1-hour loads were about 2.4–2.7 in GS, LD, and HD, and 1.4 in HA. The 10-hour estimates were ordered GS (9.6), LD (5.9), HA (4.1), and HD (3.3). The 100-hour estimates followed the same order, from 19.6 (95% CI 11.8 to 32.8) in GS to 7.5 (95% CI 4.6 to 12.2) in HD. Post-PCT 1,000-hour means ranged from 25.2 in HA to 53.9 in GS, with wide confidence intervals. These rankings describe estimated loads; they do not establish pairwise treatment differences. The separate dead-fuel phase estimates are reference conditions, without paired phase-change tests in this display.


Standing vegetation and woody vegetation difference
Pre-PCT woody standing-vegetation means were greatest in GS (39.9), followed by LD (26.5), HD (18.8), and HA (14.7). Post-PCT means were 2.0–2.9 across treatments. The joint phase model estimated pre-minus-post reductions of 37.4 (95% CI 13.4 to 61.4) in GS, 24.5 (95% CI 9.0 to 40.0) in LD, 11.8 (95% CI 3.6 to 20.0) in HA, and 16.6 (95% CI 5.5 to 27.6) in HD. All four reduction intervals excluded zero. Their uncertainty includes the pre/post covariance; the ordering of reduction estimates alone does not test differences among treatments.
Herbaceous standing-vegetation means were small relative to woody loads: 0.24–0.59 before PCT and 0.11–0.35 afterward, with broad relative uncertainty. The woody reduction represents an inferred potential contribution to surface fuels. It does not measure slash deposition or reconcile standing-vegetation loss with changes in downed fuel classes. Without a contemporaneous unthinned comparison, the phase transition does not isolate a causal PCT effect.


Fuel inventory








Figure 2: Fuel components by retention treatment before and after precommercial thinning (PCT). Points are site-standardized mean loads from AIC-leading models, integrated over all fitted random effects and including modeled zeros; ranges are 95% confidence intervals for the means. Study sites receive equal weights. Orange denotes pre-PCT and blue denotes post-PCT for the six components measured in both phases. Litter and duff are pre-PCT only. The woody vegetation-difference panel is the pre-PCT minus post-PCT mean contrast from the joint matched woody phase model, with its pre/post covariance. It is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load. Panel-specific y-scales are used.

title: Introduction
text:
Introduction
Developing and maintaining multiaged stand structures requires silvicultural systems that create and sustain cohorts of different ages within the same stand (O’Hara, 1998; Schütz, 2002). Retention systems can retain a range of tree densities in dispersed or aggregated patterns and can be used to maintain multiaged stands or transform formerly even-aged stands (Mitchell & Beese, 2002).
Coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) is well suited to this objective because it regenerates reliably by stump sprouting and can grow beneath a retained overstory. Its response to light is nevertheless important: reduced access to light can limit sprout vigor and persistence (Berrill et al., 2018; Muma et al., 2022; O’Hara et al., 2007). Tanoak (Notholithocarpus densiflorus) is also shade tolerant and a vigorous resprouter, making its response relevant to both stand development and management of competing vegetation (Berrill et al., 2021; O’Hara et al., 2017).
Silvicultural decisions that promote regeneration also influence the fuel conditions in which later management and fire occur. This paper therefore examines regeneration under varying overstory retention and describes surface fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning as reference information for integrated silvicultural, fuels, fire, and potential modeling applications.
We use 10-year measurements from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment to evaluate regeneration responses among retention treatments and to report fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including their PCT-associated contrast. Redwood and tanoak provide the primary regeneration focus, with other species retained as descriptive context where useful. Fuel components will be presented in a publication-specific form after their analytical specification is reviewed.
